issue.issue_text: Whether retention of official accommodation by the functionaries mentioned in Section 4(3) of the 1981 Act after they had demitted office violate the equality clause guaranteed by Article 14 of the Constitution of India.

facts: Section 4(3) of the Uttar Pradesh Ministers (Salaries, Allowances and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1981, was amended in 2016 to allow former Chief Ministers of the State to be allotted government accommodation for their lifetime.
A writ petition was filed challenging the constitutional validity of this provision.
The Supreme Court had previously struck down similar rules (the 1997 Rules) that provided the same benefit, finding them unfair and violative of the Constitution.
law: Article 14 of the Constitution of India guarantees equality and prohibits unreasonable classification.
Public property, such as government bungalows, is a scarce natural resource that belongs to the people and must be allocated based on principles of equality, justice, and fairness.
Any law creating a special class of citizens is subject to judicial review on the touchstone of Article 14 to determine if the classification is reasonable and not arbitrary.
application: The Court reasoned that once a Chief Minister demits office, they are on par with any common citizen. The public office they once held becomes a "matter of history."

Section 4(3) creates a separate class of citizens for the benefit of public property based on a past position, which is not a reasonable basis for classification. Therefore, the law fails the "test of reasonable classification."
The Court found that there is nothing to distinguish former Chief Ministers from the common person that would justify the special privilege of a lifetime government bungalow.
The legislation was deemed arbitrary and discriminatory, as it used irrelevant considerations to distribute scarce public property intended for current officeholders.
The Court also viewed the amendment as an attempt to overreach its prior judgment that had already invalidated similar rules.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that Section 4(3) of the 1981 Act violates the equality clause under Article 14 of the Constitution. Consequently, the Court declared the provision unconstitutional (ultra vires) and struck it down.

cases.case_name: Indian Express Newspapers (Bombay) (P) Ltd. v. Union of India
cases.principle: The test of manifest arbitrariness applies to invalidate legislation as well as subordinate legislation under Article 14. Manifest arbitrariness is something done by the legislature capriciously, irrationally, without adequate determining principle, or is excessive and disproportionate.
Article 14 condemns discrimination not only by a substantive law but also by a law of procedure.

If an impugned State action is arbitrary and therefore violative of Article 14, it can be struck down irrespective of whether an additional contractual or statutory right is also available to the aggrieved persons.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The State is the legal owner of natural resources as a trustee of the people, and the process of distributing these resources must be guided by constitutional principles, including the doctrine of equality and the larger public good. Article 14 of the Constitution condemns discrimination resulting from both substantive and procedural laws.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The retention of official accommodation by functionaries after they have demitted office creates a special class of citizens, which is abhorrent to the constitutional ethos of equality and fraternity. In a democratic republic where ultimate authority vests in the citizens, any privileges or benefits conferred on holders of public office must be reasonable, rational, and proportionate. Allowing former officials to retain public property, which is held by the State in trust for the people, amounts to an arbitrary and discriminatory distribution of State largesse that is not in the public interest and violates the equality clause under Article 14 of the Constitution.
legal_tests_applied: Manifest Arbitrariness Test: Legislation can be negated under Article 14 if it is manifestly arbitrary.

Public Trust Doctrine: The State is the legal owner of natural and public resources as a trustee of the people, and the process of distribution must be guided by constitutional principles including the doctrine of equality and larger public good.
Reasonableness, Rationality, and Proportionality Test: All privileges, rights, and benefits conferred on holders of public office must be reasonable, rational, and proportionate.
Fair Distribution of State Largesse: The distribution of State-owned property and resources must be fair, equitable, guided by public interest, and free from arbitrariness, favouritism, or nepotism.
why_respondent_won: The creation of a special class of citizens who can retain public accommodation after demitting office is abhorrent to the constitutional principles of equality and fraternity embodied in the Preamble.
The permanent retention of such privileges is incompatible with the sovereign, republican, and egalitarian form of government, much like the privy purses for former rulers were found to be.
In a democratic republic, public servants are accountable to the citizens, and this requires a framework of equality where benefits are not disproportionate or irrational.

State-owned property is held in trust for the people and must be distributed to serve the common good and public interest, not the private interests of former functionaries. Any departure from this rule must be for rational reasons, not suggestive of discrimination.

Allowing former officials to retain accommodation is an arbitrary distribution of State largesse, which gives an appearance of bias, jobbery, or nepotism, violating the principle that public justice must not only be done but also be seen to be done.
policy_considerations: Holders of public office should take decisions solely in terms of the public interest and should not do so in order to gain financial or other material benefits for themselves, their family, or their friends.

It is axiomatic that in a democratic republican government, public servants entrusted with duties of public nature must act in a manner that reflects that ultimate authority is vested in the citizens.
Material resources of the community must be distributed to sub-serve the common good and the constitutional objective of securing socio-economic justice.
The appearance of public justice is as important as doing justice, and nothing should be done which gives an appearance of bias, jobbery or nepotism.
